summary: The English of 3:1-3:6 is mostly sound, but in three places it goes against the normative commentators: וְיִדֹּם in 3:2 (Bartenura and Rambam read a low voice of study, not silence), the third proof in 3:6 (both read אֱלֹהִים as judges), and 3:4, where Bartenura reads the idle heart as the condition of the night and the lonely road. The senses were filled mechanically: almost every token had sense 1, which is often a bare header, the Qal for a Nifal or Piel, or a wrong homograph (Heshbon, Ramah, Shem, Sacar, Zebah, 'lamb' for זֶה, 'no, not' for אֶל and אֵל, 'father' for בָּא); these are moved to the right entries the pack lists or removed. Several commentary summaries misstate the comment (Bartenura 3:3:5, 3:6:4, 3:6:5; Rambam on the Commander), some learner notes are untrue (בְּלָעוֹ as infinitive, 'chiastic', 'three imperatives'), and the Vilna verse numbers were not recorded. The model morphology has wrong states (construct/absolute) on עֹל, לֵצִים, סֵפֶר, מְקוֹם, מָקוֹם, wrong binyan on וַיַּקְשֵׁב, wrong analyses of בְּלָעוֹ and עָתִיד, and a few form spellings.

value: The saying has the form of a question and an answer: one imperative, דַּע 'know', governs three questions, and each is then answered in turn.
אִי אַתָּה בָא is the Mishnaic negative with a participle (a future: 'you will not come'); אִי stands for אֵין.
עָתִיד is an adjective (the pattern qatil), 'ready, destined', and takes the infinitive לִתֵּן: 'you are destined to give'.
מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים is a double superlative ('King of the kings of kings'): the construct chain piles up the title.
מֵאַיִן, וּלְאָן and וְלִפְנֵי מִי are three interrogative phrases, each repeated in the answer; the third answer reuses the whole question.
patches.reason: Two notes were untrue: there is one imperative דַּע, not three; עָתִיד is an adjective, not a participle (the Qal participle would be עוֹתֵד).

patches.value: עָתִיד, an adjective: 'ready, destined, about to'; with לְ + infinitive, 'destined to'.
patches.reason: The morphology is corrected to adjective; the note says so.

value: Vilna reads עבירה for עֲבֵרָה, and ליתן for לִתֵּן (twice): spellings only.

Rabbeinu Yonah on 3:1 links the first consideration (whence you came) to lowliness of spirit, which saves from pride (Proverbs 16:5, cited there as 16:4), the second (dust and worm) to contempt for pleasures and wealth, as in Ecclesiastes, and the third to the shame of the soul before the King of kings.
patches.reason: The line said Rabbeinu Yonah links all three considerations to humility; he links only the first to humility, the second to contempt for pleasures, the third to the fear and shame before God.

patches.value: Rabbi Hanina, the deputy of the priests, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear of it, each man would have swallowed his fellow alive. Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion says: Two who sit with no words of Torah between them, this is a seat of scoffers, as it is said (Psalm 1): "and in the seat of scoffers he has not sat." But two who sit with words of Torah between them, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the LORD and for those who esteem his name." I know this only of two. From where do we learn that even for one who sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets a reward for him? As it is said (Lamentations 3): "He sits alone and murmurs, for he has taken it upon himself."
patches.reason: Bartenura (3:2:4: לְשׁוֹן קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַּקָּה, the whisper of one who studies alone) and Rambam (3:2:2: הַדִּבּוּר הַנִּסְתָּר, quiet speech) agree that וְיִדֹּם here is a low voice of study, not silence; the proof depends on it.

value: The verse has three sayings: Rabbi Hanina the deputy on prayer for the government, Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion on Torah study in company, and its extension to one who studies alone.
שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא introduces a contrafactual clause; the apodosis is the perfect בְּלָעוֹ (בָּלַע with the suffix -וֹ, resuming רֵעֵהוּ): 'would have swallowed him'.
שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן ... is a casus pendens: 'Two who sit and there is not between them ... this is ...'; הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause.
וְיֵשׁ and וְאֵין are the existential particles ('there is' and 'there is not') followed by a subject in the construct: 'words of Torah'.
מִנַּיִן is the standard Talmudic question, 'from where (do we learn)'; the answers are verses, quoted by their source.
patches.reason: The note called בְּלָעוֹ an infinitive; it is the Qal perfect with a suffix.

patches.value: סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים is 'the deputy of the priests'; the English keeps the title. מַלְכוּת is 'the government' (the sages read the ruling power, including foreign rule: Bartenura 3:2:1). The sentence 'each man would have swallowed his fellow alive' (Bartenura 3:2:2 cites Habakkuk 1:14, 'like the fish of the sea') is a contrafactual. The last verse, נָטַל עָלָיו, is read in the Mishnah as 'he has taken it upon himself': Bartenura 3:2:5 reads 'as though the whole giving of the Torah were for him alone'; וְיִדֹּם is rendered 'murmurs': Bartenura (3:2:4) and Rambam (3:2:2) read it as the soft voice of one who studies in a whisper; Rabbeinu Yonah reads silent study in thought. In Lamentations 3:28 the verse is more likely 'Let him sit alone and be silent, for he has laid it upon him' (God has laid it on him).
patches.reason: The note must follow the English change on וְיִדֹּם.

value.summary: Bartenura: וְיִדֹּם is 'a term of a still, thin voice' (קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַּקָּה), the way one who studies alone studies in a whisper. The English follows with 'murmurs'.

patches.reason: With Rambam agreeing, the English now follows this reading.

patches.value: Rambam (anchored here by the pack, but commenting on 3:1) says that looking at whence one came brings humility, looking at one's end brings contempt for worldly affairs, and looking to the greatness of the One who commands (הַמְצַוֶּה) brings haste to obey His commandments; one who holds these three will not sin at all. This bears on 3:1, not on the plain sense of 3:2.
patches.reason: גּוֹדֶל הַמְצַוֶּה, followed by מִצְוֹתָיו 'His commandments', is the greatness of the Commander (the King before whom one gives account), not 'the commandment'.

value.summary: Rabbeinu Yonah: the one who is silent and meditates in Torah is as if he took upon himself the yoke of Torah in thought; he cites the Rama's reading, that one who studies alone is as if he fulfilled the whole Torah, with וְיִדֹּם as speech.

patches.reason: Records the real alternative to the English 'murmurs' (silent study in thought).

value: Psalm 1:1 (the last clause, וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵצִים לֹא יָשָׁב).
Malachi 3:16 (אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ ...): the Mishnah quotes the verse to its end; the proof is in אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ, two speakers.
Lamentations 3:28 (יֵשֵׁב בָּדָד וְיִדֹּם כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו).
Vilna reads ה for יְיָ (three times), ולחושבי for וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי, שאפילו for שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ, וידום for וְיִדֹּם; Vilna omits שְׁרוּיָה ('dwells') at 3:2.48.
3:2.34 תהלים, 3:2.51 מלאכי and 3:2.88 איכה are the source names of the quoted verses; 3:2.35, 3:2.52 and 3:2.89 are letter numerals for the chapters.
Vilna adds the verse number after each source: (תהלים א) א, (מלאכי ג) טז, (איכה ג) כח.
patches.reason: The Malachi line was garbled ('the spoken words are those who fear the LORD'); the three Vilna additions of verse numbers (variants with no base token) were not recorded.

patches.value: Bartenura: as soon as one speaks words of Torah, the table is called 'the table that is before the LORD'. Some say the proof is from the head of the verse, 'the altar of wood, three cubits (אַמּוֹת)': read not אַמּוֹת but אִמּוֹת, 'mothers' (sources), three, for Torah, Prophets and Writings (or Scripture, Mishnah and Talmud), which a man must speak of at the table; so Rashi explained. The English follows the first reading.
patches.reason: The summary said he derives 'the three-cubit altar from the three parts of Scripture'; it is the reverse: the three parts of Scripture to be spoken at the table are derived from 'three cubits', read אִמּוֹת.

Ezekiel 41:22 (the last words: זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי יְיָ); the Mishnah's text of Ezekiel runs וַיְדַבֵּר אֵלַי.

patches.value: Rabbi Hanina son of Hakhinai says: One who is awake at night, or who walks on the road alone, and who turns his heart to idleness: this one is answerable with his life.
patches.reason: Bartenura, the only normative comment here, reads the third clause as the condition of the first two: the one awake at night or walking alone who thinks idle thoughts (3:4:1 וּמְחַשֵּׁב בְּלִבּוֹ דִּבְרֵי הֲבַאי), because night and the lonely road are dangerous and Torah would guard him (3:4:2). Rabbeinu Yonah reads the same. Three independent subjects make the waking and the journey themselves liable.

One who is awake at night
or who walks on the road alone
value.literal: 'and-the-one-walking on-the-road alone'; the second situation, alternative to the first

value.english: and who turns his heart to idleness
value.literal: 'and-the-one-clearing his-heart to-idleness'; Bartenura reads this clause as the condition of both situations

patches.reason: The English changed (Bartenura's reading).

patches.value: מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ is rendered 'is answerable with his life'. The English follows Bartenura: the night (3:4:1-2) is the time of demons and the lone traveller is in danger from robbers and other harm, and the one in either case who turns his heart to idle thoughts is guilty, for words of Torah would have guarded him. Read grammatically as three separate subjects, each participle with its own article, the saying would make the waking and the journey liable by themselves; the commentators do not read it so.
patches.reason: The note said Bartenura makes 'the three' guilty when they also think idle thoughts; he applies the idle thoughts to the first two cases.

value: Three participles with the article (הַנֵּעוֹר, הַמְהַלֵּךְ, הַמְפַנֶּה) head the sentence; Bartenura reads the third as the condition of the first two: one who is awake at night or walks alone, and turns his heart to idle things.
הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause ('this one ...'), resuming the subject.
הַנֵּעוֹר is a Nifal participle of עור, 'is awake'; מְהַלֵּךְ and מְפַנֶּה are Piel participles. The Piel of פנה is 'to clear, make room': he frees his heart for idleness.
מִתְחַיֵּב is a Hitpael participle: 'makes himself liable'. The Vilna spelling is מתחייב.
בְּנַפְשׁוֹ 'with his life': he puts his own life at risk (Bartenura: demons by night, robbers on the road).
יְחִידִי, 'alone, by himself', is the Mishnaic adverbial form of יָחִיד.
patches.reason: The first note took the three participles as three independent subjects against Bartenura; the note on יְחִידִי ('old adverbial ending') is not supported; the Piel of פנה is now explained.

patches.value: יְחִידִי, the Mishnaic adverbial form of יָחִיד: 'alone, by himself'.
patches.reason: 'the old ending -י' is not a known ending; the form is simply the Mishnaic adverb.

patches.value: Piel participle of פנה 'to clear, make room': he empties his heart for idle things.
patches.reason: The Piel of פנה is 'to clear', not 'to turn aside' (the Qal); the English 'turns his heart' keeps the idiom.

value.summary: Bartenura: the one awake at night and the one walking alone on the road are guilty when he thinks idle things in his heart (וּמְחַשֵּׁב בְּלִבּוֹ דִּבְרֵי הֲבַאי): the third clause is the condition of the first two. The English follows.

patches.reason: The ruling said 'the three are guilty when they also think idle thoughts' and recorded the reading; Bartenura qualifies the first two cases, and the English now follows him.

patches.value: Bartenura: night is the time of demons, and one who walks alone on the road is in danger from robbers and many evils; had he thought of words of Torah, it would have guarded him. Hence he is liable with his life only when his heart is turned to idleness. The English follows.
patches.reason: States the consequence of his reason for the reading of the clauses.

value: The saying is two parallel conditional sentences: כָּל + participle, then a plural participle (מַעֲבִירִין, נוֹתְנִין) as an impersonal passive.
The two sentences are antithetic and in the same order: the one who takes the yoke of Torah has the other yokes removed (מַעֲבִירִין), the one who throws it off has them placed on him (נוֹתְנִין).
הַמְקַבֵּל and הַפּוֹרֵק are articular participles used as the subject after כָּל, 'whoever takes / whoever throws off'; קִבֵּל עָלָיו and פָּרַק מִמֶּנּוּ are the opposite idioms for a yoke.
עֹל תּוֹרָה is a construct chain 'the yoke of Torah'; the same pattern, עֹל מַלְכוּת, עֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, follows.
דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ ('the way of the land') is an idiom for the ordinary business of life, and in Avot often for the worldly occupation of earning a living.
patches.reason: The sentences are parallel, not chiastic (the order is the same in both), and there is no pun: the notes must be true for a learner.

patches.value: Rabbi Halafta son of Dosa, of Kefar Hananiah, says: Ten who sit and occupy themselves with Torah, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Psalm 82): "God stands in the congregation of God." And from where even five? As it is said (Amos 9): "and his bundle upon the earth he has founded." And from where even three? As it is said (Psalm 82): "In the midst of judges he judges." And from where even two? As it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and so on." And from where even one? As it is said (Exodus 20): "In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you."
patches.reason: Bartenura (3:6:3-4, the three judges, שֶׁהַדַּיָּנִים הֵם שְׁלֹשָׁה) and Rambam (3:6:1, a court of no fewer than three, called אֱלֹהִים for judgment) agree that אֱלֹהִים here means judges; the proof for three rests on it.

patches.value: The proof of the five rests on אֲגֻדָּתוֹ, 'his bundle': Rambam and Rabbeinu Yonah read a bundle as what one binds in one hand, which has five fingers. Bartenura's own text reverses the two middle proofs: five from 'in the midst of judges he judges' (three judges and two litigants) and three from 'his bundle' (fire, air and water around the earth, or three stalks of hyssop); he gives the order of this text as the reading of 'some books', with the hand of five fingers. The English keeps 'his bundle'. In the first proof the congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten (Rambam; Bartenura from the spies, Numbers 14:27). In the third, אֱלֹהִים is 'judges' (a court of three: Rambam, Bartenura), and the English follows them. 'Kefar Hananiah' is a place, as in the pack. The pack's lemma link for אֵל (the particle אַל) does not fit; the word is אֵל 'God', in 'the congregation of God'.
patches.reason: The note said the English keeps 'God' in the third proof; it also misstated Bartenura's order of proofs.

patches.value: Bartenura (his heading reads 'and from where even five' with this verse): 'in the midst of judges he judges' gives three judges and two litigants, five. The English follows the base text, which proves three from this verse, as Bartenura himself explains in the reading of 'some books' (3:6:4); his own order is recorded here.
patches.reason: The summary quoted the verse as 'in the midst of God' and did not say that his heading attaches this verse to five.

patches.value: Bartenura's text reads 'even three' with 'his bundle': fire, air and water, three, surround the foundation of the earth; or a bundle of hyssop of three stalks. He adds that some books read 'even five' with this verse, for a man binds with one hand of five fingers, and the whole of the fingers is called a bundle; the head of the verse, 'who builds His upper chambers in the heavens', means that the Shekhinah descends when a bundle studies Torah; and then 'even three' from 'in the midst of judges', for judges are three. The English follows the 'some books' reading, which is the base text.
patches.reason: The summary did not say which number his own text attaches to Amos 9:6, nor that the English follows the reading he gives for 'some books'.

patches.value: Bartenura: נָטַל עָלָיו is a term of covering (לְשׁוֹן סְכָךְ), as the Targum renders וְסַכֹּתָ 'and you shall cover' by וְתַטֵּל: the Shekhinah covers him. The comment belongs to the verse of 3:2 (Lamentations 3:28), not to the plain sense of 3:6.
patches.reason: The summary said נָטַל is 'from the root of סכך'; Bartenura says it is a term for covering, by the Targum's rendering, not that it shares a root.

patches.value: Rambam: a congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten, and a court not fewer than three, who are called אֱלֹהִים for judgment; an אֲגֻדָּה is what a man binds with one hand, which has five fingers, so the five fingers are called a bundle. The English follows all three points: 'congregation', 'judges' and 'his bundle'.
patches.reason: The ruling said the English follows only the first point; with 'judges' it now follows all three.
